stances.claim: Fidel V. Ramos is 'arguably the Best President of the Republic' -- first/only Protestant President of Catholic PH, only general to ascend to constitutional 'Commander in Chief,' equipped with a grand vision of 'Philippines 2000.'

stances.claim: FVR's nonpartisan-Cabinet philosophy -- 'I want to be president of all the people, not only of those who voted for me' -- was demonstrated by his invitation to CJ Panganiban (who had voted for Salonga, not FVR) and to Henrietta De Villa.

stances.claim: FVR respected CJ's independence throughout his 11+ years on the Court -- never influencing him 'directly or indirectly,' never voicing displeasure even when CJ voted against FVR's perceived wishes or authored a contrary decision.

CJ owes his SC appointment 'solely to President Ramos' -- 'to him only, as I had no padrinos or sponsors' -- making the appointment a direct presidential decision based on Rotary-Club observation, not patronage.
FVR is 'truly, a gentleman of the highest caliber' -- the closing characterological verdict on a six-year presidential relationship and twenty-plus-year personal one.

notable_anecdotes: June 16, 1992: CJ, on his way to a Manila City Hall court hearing, receives a surprise call on his 'huge, extra heavy mobile phone connected to my car' -- the caller introduces himself: 'Is this Attorney Art Panganiban? This is Eddie.' CJ, irritated that a stranger has his private number, asks, 'Eddie who?' -- to be told 'Eddie Ramos.'

The June 17, 1992 meeting at the white-door office marked simply '202,' 845 Pasay Road, Makati -- opened by Joe Almonte ('I am Joe Almonte. Please come in. The President is waiting for you.') who ushers CJ to a big conference room with only the President-elect and CJ in attendance.

FVR initially offered the Secretary of Justice post, also inviting Henrietta 'Tita' De Villa as a Catholic lay leader -- CJ politely declined because he had 'not campaigned for you' and 'voted for your mentor Jovy Salonga.'

FVR's reply rebutting CJ's hesitation: 'I know you did not campaign for me. You did not even vote for me. You voted for your mentor Jovy Salonga. But that's alright. I want to have a nonpartisan Cabinet. I want to be president of all the people, not only of those who voted for me.'

FVR's Rotary recollection ('Munching his unlighted tobacco'): the 1990-1991 CJ presidency vision 'Love God, Serve Man,' 78 printed-manual projects with budget and timeline, valedictory spreadsheet report, standing ovation -- used as evidence of CJ's executive capability.
CJ declined Justice secretary but happily accepted associate justice of the Supreme Court -- 'I owe my appointment solely to President Ramos (to him only, as I had no padrinos or sponsors).'

FVR's June 30, 1998 farewell letter: 'On behalf of the Philippine government and the Filipino people, I wish to convey to you my deepest appreciation and gratitude for the exemplary service, professionalism, and deep commitment to our people's well-being and national interest...'

one_paragraph_summary: On March 18, 2024 -- Fidel V. Ramos's 96th birthday -- Panganiban reminisces about the only president to whom he owes his appointment to the Supreme Court. He frames FVR with three superlatives: 'first and only Protestant President of Catholic Philippines,' 'only general to ascend to the constitutional title Commander in Chief of all armed forces of the Philippines,' and 'arguably, the Best President of the Republic, complete with a grand vision of Philippines 2000.' He then narrates the story of how he was 'plucked ... from anonymity' and conscripted 'without passing through the judicial ladder.' On June 16, 1992 -- after the election but before FVR assumed office on June 30 -- CJ, en route to a Manila City Hall court hearing, received a surprise call on his 'huge, extra heavy mobile phone connected to my car': 'Is this Attorney Art Panganiban? This is Eddie.' CJ, irritated, asked, 'Eddie who?' -- and was told 'Eddie Ramos.' The next morning at 7 a.m., CJ knocked at the white door of office '202,' 845 Pasay Road, Makati, where Joe Almonte ushered him to a one-on-one with the President-elect. After an hour of exchanging views, FVR offered him the Secretary of Justice post (also inviting Henrietta 'Tita' De Villa). CJ declined because he had not campaigned for FVR and had voted for his mentor Jovy Salonga; FVR replied, 'I know you did not campaign for me. You did not even vote for me. You voted for your mentor Jovy Salonga. But that's alright. I want to have a nonpartisan Cabinet. I want to be president of all the people, not only of those who voted for me' -- then, 'Munching his unlighted tobacco,' recalled CJ's 1990-1991 Rotary Club of Manila presidency with its 'Love God, Serve Man' vision, 78 printed-manual projects with budget and timeline, and valedictory spreadsheet report, telling him, 'Quite impressive.' CJ ultimately declined Justice secretary but happily accepted associate justice of the Supreme Court -- 'I owe my appointment solely to President Ramos (to him only, as I had no padrinos or sponsors).' FVR respected CJ's independence throughout the 11+ Court years, never voicing or hinting at displeasure even when CJ voted against perceived FVR wishes -- 'Truly, a gentleman of the highest caliber.' At the end of FVR's term on June 30, 1998, the President sent an edifying letter of gratitude, and CJ replied that he had tried to discharge his duties 'with moral courage, integrity, and dedication.' CJ's 1998 book 'Battles in the Supreme Court' was dedicated to FVR as 'Leader, Reformer, Builder, Peacemaker, and Gentleman' -- to which FVR replied, 'I may be off to see the sunset, but don't be too surprised to see me there, with you, at the next sunrise.'
